rungs.stem: In the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology, the court of King Conchobar mac Nessa at Emain Macha has three great powers: the king, the champion, and one more figure whose word is heeded by every hero. That third figure reads the fitness of days and foretells what will come. What was he called?
choices: the druid
the ollamh (chief poet)
the brehon (chief judge)
the seanchai (chief storyteller)
rungs.context: In the Ulster Cycle the druid stands beside the king and the warrior as the third of the ruling powers. The ollamh was the highest rank of poet (Amergin, for example); the brehon was the judge who spoke the ancient Brehon Laws; the seanchai was the traditional storyteller of a household. All existed, but only the druid handled prophecy and the fitness of days.

rungs.stem: In the Ulster Cycle the chief druid at the royal fort of Emain Macha runs a school for young pupils, teaching them to divine what will come to pass. He is King Conchobar mac Nessa's adviser and, in one strand of the tradition, Conchobar's own father by the warrior-woman Nessa. What is this chief druid's name?
choices: Cathbad
Amergin
Mug Ruith
Fintan
rungs.context: Cathbad is the chief druid at Emain Macha and stands beside Conchobar throughout the Ulster tales. Amergin was the great druid of the Milesian invasion who chanted the land into their possession; Mug Ruith is the huge blind wheel-riding druid of Munster; Fintan mac Bochra is the salmon-shaped survivor of the Flood in Irish tradition. All are druids, but Cathbad is the Ulster chief.

rungs.stem: The chief druid at Emain Macha teaches his pupils outside the fort one morning, reading the fitness of the day. He tells them that if any warrior takes up arms for the very first time on this day, that warrior will win FAME everlasting through Ireland. But there is a price attached to the day of arms. What is the price?
choices: he will live only a short life
he will lose the use of one eye in his first battle
he will father no son to carry his name
he will never sleep under a roof again
rungs.answer: he will live only a short life
rungs.context: Cathbad's day-of-arms prophecy is the Irish equivalent of Achilles's choice: fame or long life, not both. Losing an eye is Odin's price for wisdom in the Norse pillar; the son-less price echoes Cuchulainn's later grief over Connla; sleeping under no roof is a geis (taboo) on other heroes, not the day-of-arms condition.

rungs.stem: In the Ulster Cycle boyhood-deeds of Cu Chulainn, a boy of about seven overheard the chief druid Cathbad teaching that whoever took arms for the first time that very day would win eternal fame but live only a short life. What did the boy do the moment he heard it?
choices: ran straight to King Conchobar and demanded arms that day
hid in the woods so the day would pass without him
asked Cathbad to wait a year until he was ready
prayed to Lugh for a way to escape the fate
rungs.answer: ran straight to King Conchobar and demanded arms that day
rungs.context: The boy chose glory over long life without hesitation. This is the Irish Achilles-choice, delivered by a seven-year-old to his uncle the king. The remaining three options would be the responses of a cautious child, but the point of the tale is exactly that Cu Chulainn was not cautious. Praying to Lugh belongs to his later fights, not to this scene.

rungs.stem: When the chief druid Cathbad discovered that Conchobar had actually given weapons to the boy Setanta on the day of the short-life prophecy, he came before the king in anger. But the boy answered his rebuke with his own famous line, in the Ulster Cycle's boyhood-deeds. What did the boy say?
choices: that a short life with lasting fame is better than a long life without it
that no druid's word could bind a warrior of Ulster
that his mother had already promised the fate to him
that only the sword would tell what the day would bring
rungs.answer: that a short life with lasting fame is better than a long life without it
rungs.context: The boy's answer is the Ulster Cycle's version of the Achilles-choice speech from the Iliad and it seals his character for the rest of the Tain. Denying druid-authority is Ferghus's later stance, not the boy's here. His mother Deichtine is not part of this scene. The 'sword will tell' line is not attested.

rungs.stem: Cathbad is the chief druid of Ulster in the Ulster Cycle. In one strand of the tradition his relationship to King Conchobar mac Nessa is unusually close: Cathbad is Conchobar's own FATHER, by the warrior-woman Nessa. According to that version, how did Cathbad and Nessa first come together?
choices: Nessa asked him for what deed done that hour would bring a king, and he answered by begetting one
Nessa was won by him in single combat with her champion at the ford
Nessa served him seven years as his pupil in the druid-school
Nessa hid him for a year in her fort during his exile
rungs.answer: Nessa asked him for what deed done that hour would bring a king, and he answered by begetting one
rungs.context: In the tale of Conchobar's conception, Nessa met Cathbad and asked what an auspicious hour was for; he told her the hour was for begetting a king; she took his answer literally and lay with him, and Conchobar was born of that hour. In the OTHER main version Cathbad only raises the boy and Fachtna Fathach is the biological father. The other three options are invented for the choices.

rungs.stem: The chief druid Cathbad appears at ANOTHER birth in the Ulster Cycle -- the newborn daughter of Feidlimid, who would grow into the fairest woman in Ireland. Cathbad's prophecy over the infant terrified the whole court of Ulster, who demanded she be killed at birth. Whose birth was this?
choices: Deirdre
Medb of Connacht
Macha of the twins
Emer, wife of Cu Chulainn
rungs.context: The tale is Longes mac nUislenn, 'The Exile of the Sons of Uisliu'. Cathbad prophesied that Deirdre would bring blood, ruin, and exile on the men of Ulster. Medb is the Connacht queen who raises the Tain against Ulster; Macha (of the twins) is the goddess-figure who curses the Ulstermen with their debility; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife, and no such prophecy is attached to her birth.

rungs.stem: Cathbad prophesied at Deirdre's birth that she would bring ruin on the men of Ulster. The warriors of Ulster demanded the infant be killed at once. King Conchobar refused. What did Conchobar do with the infant Deirdre instead?
choices: had her raised in isolation so he himself could marry her when she was grown
gave her in fosterage to a smith of the border country
sent her to be reared by the druids of Emain Macha
cast her adrift in a leather bag on the western sea
rungs.answer: had her raised in isolation so he himself could marry her when she was grown
rungs.context: Conchobar's plan was to keep Deirdre hidden away with tutors and never let her see any young man until she was of age for him. She saw Naoise anyway, one of the sons of Uisliu, and eloped with him -- which set off the tragedy Cathbad had foretold. The smith-fosterage recalls the Setanta / Culann story; druid-fosterage is Finn Emna's youth in a different tale; the leather bag on the sea is the birth-exposure of Taliesin in the Welsh tradition.

rungs.stem: The men of Ulster's greatest warrior went into exile at the court of Queen Medb of Connacht after Conchobar treacherously killed the sons of Uisliu -- the very ruin Cathbad had foretold over the newborn Deirdre. This is why he then leads the Connacht army against his own former Ulster people in the great cattle-raid of the Tain Bo Cuailnge. Which warrior was he?
choices: Fergus mac Roich
Conall Cernach
Loegaire Buadach
Sualtam mac Roich
rungs.context: Fergus mac Roich had guaranteed safe conduct to the sons of Uisliu, and Conchobar's treachery in killing them dishonoured Fergus so utterly that he left Ulster forever. In the Tain he is the great Ulster exile in Medb's army. Conall Cernach and Loegaire Buadach stayed with Ulster and fought for Conchobar. Sualtam is Cu Chulainn's mortal father, not an exile.

rungs.stem: In the Ulster Cycle, Cathbad's prophecies do not merely PREDICT what will come; they SHAPE what comes -- once spoken, every hero acts to fulfil them, thinking he is choosing freely. Which other prophet in the wider Western tradition is most closely paralleled by Cathbad in exactly this way, warning of dooms whose warnings are the means by which the dooms come to pass?
choices: Tiresias in Greek tragedy
Saint John of Patmos writing Revelation
the Norns weaving under Yggdrasil
the sibyl at Cumae guiding Aeneas
rungs.context: Tiresias warns Oedipus and Odysseus and Creon of dooms that come precisely because he warned them; every act to escape the warning fulfils it. The Norns weave fate silently and do not warn heroes to their faces. Saint John of Patmos writes visions of the end of the world, not personal warnings to a hero. The sibyl at Cumae guides Aeneas THROUGH the underworld but does not deliver doom-prophecies of his death. Merlin in the Arthurian tradition is the closest Western parallel to Cathbad if one were needed inside this bank's own pillars.
